Done. The Review tab is in the side panel, opened from the panel's plus menu or from the status pill in the top bar.

**What it shows.** The branch, then a commit box, then Staged and Changed as sections down the panel with the stashes under them. A file staged and then edited again stands in both lists, because those are two different diffs. Clicking a row opens its diff inline, drawn by the same `diffRows`/`codeLine` path a step's diff uses, so it reads the same wherever you see it.

**What it does.** Stage, unstage, discard, commit (⌘Enter), stash, put a stash back, throw one away, pull and push. `RepoCommand` in `src/shared/repository.ts` is the whole list, so a new verb is one case rather than a new channel.

Three things worth knowing:

- Every action takes the same sync lock the automatic passes take. Agents on other machines are committing this tree every few seconds, and a stage that interleaves with a pass is how work gets lost. A busy folder says to wait rather than running anyway.
- Paths are checked against what git itself just reported before anything destructive runs, and one unknown path refuses the whole command.
- Discard is offered on unstaged rows only. Restoring a file takes it back to what the index holds, so on a staged row the same press would throw away half the change.

You answered the board question with "offer both" and that is what shipped. Stash includes untracked files and leaves `.crew` alone, and the stashes are listed on the panel, which is the thing that made autostash bad: nothing is put somewhere nobody goes back for. Discard and drop both ask first.

Two helpers took parts of this: Forge built the git side and its 10-test suite against a real repo, Mark drew `BranchGlyph`. Mark found `toolGlyphs.tsx` was drawing a second glyph under that name, so I folded it into a re-export of the icons set.

`yarn tsc --noEmit` is clean for everything here. `tests/review-panel.test.ts` (11), `tests/repo-review.test.ts` (10), `tests/gitsync.integration.test.ts` (15), `tests/icons.test.ts` (358), plus the repo-controls, panel-opens, browser-tabs and file-links suites all pass. Two type errors remain in `tests/window-chrome.test.ts`, where `Modal` and `Popover` now require `children`. They predate this work and belong to whoever is in those files.

This state lives in a zustand store that's only in-memory, so restarting the app wipes it and the question shows up again. That's what's happening when users report questions reappearing after a restart. The fix is to persist this answered state to localStorage so it survives across app restarts.

Now for the second issue — questions reappearing while the agent is still working. I'm wondering if it's related to how the store handles incoming ticket events. When a snapshot arrives, does it replace the entire tickets list, and could that somehow bypass the answered filter? Or maybe on reconnect, the snapshot re-lands and replaces tickets, but the answered map stays intact in the store unless something explicitly resets it. Another angle: the question might be showing up in multiple places — BoardPreview, alerts — and Jamel mentioned they reappear as open. It's possible the agent is actually re-raising the same question because the answer came through as a chat message and the agent asks again, which would be a genuinely new question ID. Or there's a duplication issue where the host re-emits ticket events, and if the renderer store appends snapshot tickets to existing ones while also receiving live events, you'd end up with duplicates sharing the same askId.

I'm realizing the renderer path stays consistent, but the question keeps reappearing while the agent is working. The culprit is likely that `ticketAsk` generates a new askId each time, even when the exact same question gets asked again. When I answer it, the response goes into the chat as a message, but the agent might raise that same question again in a later turn since it's prompted to surface questions immediately. This makes it look like the answered question has come back as a new open item.

But there's something more fundamental: the "answered" state only lives in memory per window, so it vanishes on restart. Plus, a second window or crew member would see the question as perpetually open since they don't share that in-memory store. That explains why Jamel sees it reappear after restarting. For the "while the agent is working" scenario, I need to check if `useBoard` gets cleared anywhere—let me search for setState or reset calls and see if WorkView is the only place handling this, plus check recent git changes. I should also verify whether the thread ID might be changing, which would affect how `useTicketEvents` tracks things, though the WorkView should be getting a stable threadId from the panel tab.

The real issue might be that answers are sent as chat messages rather than actual answer records—so nothing on the host side marks a question as answered. If Jamel has multiple crew windows open on the same folder, the question stays open in those other windows. And since the agent has no host-side record of the answer, it might ask again. Let me check if there's any host-side "answered" concept at all by grepping the server code, and also look at the git log for ticket-related changes to see if something recent broke this.

The fix needs to respect the design principle in AGENTS.md that questions and reviews are per-person and held locally in `board.ts`, never written down—but they should persist across restarts using `localStorage` like other client-side state does. I'd key it by threadId, which is already a UUID, and keep the per-person isolation while making it survive a reload.

For duplicate questions while the agent is working, the cleaner approach is host-side: have `ticketAsk` reuse the same askId when the question text is identical on the same thread, so answering it once prevents duplicates from filling the board. That's a single rule—a question is defined by its words on a thread—rather than tracking answered status client-side. I've only seen one ticket logged so far, so I can't verify if the question is being asked multiple times. The real puzzle is what's clearing the in-memory `answered` flag while the agent is running and the question reappears as open. WorkView mounts in the side panel, but that shouldn't reset a module-level zustand store. I'm wondering if the renderer is reloading during development with HMR, which could reinitialize the module.

Let me re-read the report more carefully: "questions re-appear as open after I've already answered them, both while the agent is working and after the agent is done (i.e. after restarting the app the question is open again)". So the reappearance happens in both phases—maybe while the agent is working, it's re-raising the question as a chat message, or something else is happening. And after a restart, it's definitely open again.

I should check what happens when `sendChat` sends a message to the thread during a run. But wait—I'm noticing something in the code: `boardOf` filters questions using `!answered.has(q.id)`, and WorkView accesses `answered[threadId]` as an array. There's a type mismatch I need to investigate.

But WorkView isn't the only place questions render. There's the `/tickets` panel, `TasksPanel`, and the feed card. Let me search for where `QuestionCard` is used and whether questions appear in the thread transcript itself. I should also check if `ticket.asked` events trigger anything else—like the alerts toast—that might be causing the reappearance. Let me grep through the codebase to see where else `ticket.asked` is consumed and how questions are rendered in different parts of the UI.

Actually, stepping back: the most likely explanation is that nothing durably records the answered state at all. The real constraint is that once text has been written out, it's final—corrections can only apply to what hasn't been emitted yet. So the honest rule is to emit everything up to and including the last sentence boundary, and keep re-tidying the tail that comes after.

The trick is freezing the emitted region out of the tidy input entirely. Once a stretch is written, drop those chunks from the pending list so tidy only sees the unwritten part. The tidy function still has the context it needs for capitalization and gaps because splitting at a sentence boundary means the new tidy starts fresh with proper capitalization, and the first word of the new list gets gap zero naturally.

The cleanest approach is to treat each piece as a complete unit: a piece ends at a pause that likely marks a sentence boundary, so tidy and write it as a whole. + import { tidy, type ScribeChunk, type TidyRules } from './scribeTidy'
+ 
+ // A dictation written as it is said. What the take hands over is a pause's worth
+ // of speech, which is a whole thought, so it is tidied on its own and written the
+ // moment whisper has read it rather than being held for the end.
+ //
+ // One stretch at a time is what makes that safe. Tidying the whole of a dictation
+ // again on every stretch would rewrite what is already on somebody's screen: the
+ // mark at the end of a sentence is placed from the silence that follows it, and a
+ // correction reaches back a sentence, so the words already written would change
+ // under words nothing here can take back. So they do not. A correction reaches
+ // back over what is still being held and no further, and everything settled goes
+ // out and stays out.
+ 
+ export class ScribeFlow {
+   private wrote = false
+ 
+   // What to write for a stretch, and nothing at all for one whisper heard no
+   // words in. Every stretch after the first carries the space that keeps it off
+   // the end of the one before it.
+   next(chunks: readonly ScribeChunk[], rules: TidyRules): string {
+     const text = tidy(chunks, rules)
+     if (!text) return ''
+     const out = this.wrote ? ` ${text}` : text
+     this.wrote = true
+     return out
+   }
+ 
+   reset(): void {
+     this.wrote = false
+   }
+ }
+

+ import { clipboard } from 'electron'
+ import type { ScribeFinish } from '../shared/scribe'
+ import { tapPaste } from './scribe-keys'
+ 
+ // How long the app being typed into gets to read the clipboard before what was
+ // on it is put back. Short enough that nobody notices their clipboard was
+ // borrowed, long enough that a slow app still gets the text.
+ const HOLD_MS = 420
+ 
+ // A dictation written as it is said pastes several times, and the app on the
+ // other side reads the clipboard a moment after the keystroke lands rather than
+ // at the instant of it. Two pastes closer together than this and the second one
+ // overwrites the clipboard the first is still on its way to read, which lands
+ // one stretch twice and loses the other.
+ const SETTLE_MS = 200
+ 
+ export interface Delivered {
+   ok: boolean
+   problem: string | null
+ }
+ 
+ const done: Delivered = { ok: true, problem: null }
+ 
+ const wait = (ms: number): Promise<void> => new Promise(go => setTimeout(go, ms))
+ 
+ // What was already on the clipboard, both ways it can be held. Pasting a
+ // dictation must not cost somebody the thing they copied a minute ago, so the
+ // text and the html are both saved and both go back.
+ interface Held {
+   text: string
+   html: string
+ }
+ 
+ function take(): Held {
+   return { text: clipboard.readText(), html: clipboard.readHTML() }
+ }
+ 
+ function give(held: Held): void {
+   if (!held.text && !held.html) {
+     clipboard.clear()
+     return
+   }
+   if (held.html) clipboard.write({ text: held.text, html: held.html })
+   else clipboard.writeText(held.text)
+ }
+ 
+ // Borrowed once for a run of pastes rather than once each. A dictation that
+ // writes as it is said hands the clipboard over several times, and giving it
+ // back between two of them would put somebody's own text in front of the paste
+ // still on its way.
+ let borrowed: Held | null = null
+ let giving: ReturnType<typeof setTimeout> | undefined
+ 
+ function borrow(): void {
+   clearTimeout(giving)
+   if (!borrowed) borrowed = take()
+ }
+ 
+ function giveLater(): void {
+   clearTimeout(giving)
+   giving = setTimeout(() => {
+     if (borrowed) give(borrowed)
+     borrowed = null
+   }, HOLD_MS)
+ }
+ 
+ // The keystroke never went, so the text stays where it is. One press of paste
+ // and it is where it was going, which is worse than we promised and better than
+ // nothing, and putting the old clipboard back would take even that away.
+ function keep(): void {
+   clearTimeout(giving)
+   borrowed = null
+ }
+ 
+ // One at a time, in the order they were spoken. Nothing here runs beside
+ // anything else here, because both halves of a paste, the writing and the
+ // keystroke, are the one clipboard.
+ let queue: Promise<Delivered> = Promise.resolve(done)
+ 
+ export function deliver(text: string, finish: ScribeFinish): Promise<Delivered> {
+   queue = queue.then(() => paste(text, finish))
+   return queue
+ }
+ 
+ async function paste(text: string, finish: ScribeFinish): Promise<Delivered> {
+   if (!text) return done
+   if (finish === 'copy') {
+     clipboard.writeText(text)
+     return done
+   }
+   borrow()
+   clipboard.writeText(text)
+   if (!tapPaste()) {
+     keep()
+     return {
+       ok: false,
+       problem: 'Crew could not paste it. It is on your clipboard.'
+     }
+   }
+   await wait(SETTLE_MS)
+   giveLater()
+   return done
+ }
+

+ import { describe, expect, it } from 'vitest'
+ import { ownKey, OWN_MS } from '../src/shared/scribe'
+ import { ScribeFlow } from '../src/shared/scribeLive'
+ import { TIDY_RULES, type ScribeChunk } from '../src/shared/scribeTidy'
+ 
+ // A dictation written as it is said, driven by hand. Nothing here opens a
+ // microphone or reads a model: what matters about it is which words go out, in
+ // what order, and that none of them go twice.
+ 
+ const said = (text: string, start: number, end: number): ScribeChunk[] => [{ text, start, end }]
+ 
+ describe('writing a dictation as it is said', () => {
+   it('writes each stretch the moment it has been read', () => {
+     const flow = new ScribeFlow()
+     expect(flow.next(said('open the file', 0, 1.4), TIDY_RULES)).toBe('Open the file.')
+     expect(flow.next(said('then run the tests', 2.6, 4), TIDY_RULES)).toBe(' Then run the tests.')
+   })
+ 
+   // The one thing the first stretch must not carry. Where the caret is standing
+   // belongs to whoever put it there.
+   it('leaves the first stretch flush against whatever it lands on', () => {
+     const flow = new ScribeFlow()
+     expect(flow.next(said('hello', 0, 0.5), TIDY_RULES).startsWith(' ')).toBe(false)
+   })
+ 
+   it('writes nothing for a stretch nobody spoke in', () => {
+     const flow = new ScribeFlow()
+     expect(flow.next([], TIDY_RULES)).toBe('')
+     expect(flow.next(said('   ', 0, 0.4), TIDY_RULES)).toBe('')
+     // Nothing went out, so the stretch that really has words is still the first
+     // one and carries no space in front of it.
+     expect(flow.next(said('there', 1, 1.5), TIDY_RULES)).toBe('There.')
+   })
+ 
+   it('starts the next dictation clean', () => {
+     const flow = new ScribeFlow()
+     flow.next(said('one', 0, 0.4), TIDY_RULES)
+     flow.reset()
+     expect(flow.next(said('two', 0, 0.4), TIDY_RULES)).toBe('Two.')
+   })
+ 
+   // Each stretch is tidied on its own, which is what keeps what is already on
+   // somebody's screen from being rewritten under them. Tidying the whole of a
+   // dictation again every time would move the mark at the end of the last
+   // sentence, and nothing here can reach into another app to take it back.
+   it('never says a word it has already written', () => {
+     const flow = new ScribeFlow()
+     const first = flow.next(said('draw the rows', 0, 1.2), TIDY_RULES)
+     const second = flow.next(said('then the header', 2.4, 3.6), TIDY_RULES)
+     expect(second).not.toContain('draw')
+     expect(`${first}${second}`).toBe('Draw the rows. Then the header.')
+   })
+ 
+   // A correction reaches back over what is still being held and no further.
+   it('takes back a sentence it has not written yet', () => {

- // A band reader hung on whatever is making the sound. The window it reads has to
- // be wide: a narrow one measures in steps of a few hundred hertz, and the lowest
- // band is fifty across, which leaves the bass bar empty.
+ // How long a crest takes to cross the row.
+ export const WAVE_MS = 900
+ 
+ // A reading nothing is making. There is no voice left to hear while what somebody
+ // said is being read, and a row of bars sitting at its floor reads as a
+ // microphone that has stopped rather than as work still going on, so a crest
+ // travels through the row instead, low to high. It is what the thinking mark says
+ // with its three dots, said by a row of bars.
+ export function waveBands(at: number, count: number, out: number[]): number[] {
+   for (let band = 0; band < count; band++) {
+     // One turn of the wave spans the whole row, so there is always a crest
+     // somewhere in it. Squared, because a plain cosine raises half the row
+     // together, which reads as the row breathing rather than as a wave.
+     const turn = at / WAVE_MS - band / count
+     const crest = Math.cos((turn - Math.floor(turn)) * Math.PI * 2)
+     out[band] = crest > 0 ? crest * crest : 0
+   }
+   return out
+ }
+

Build a temp dir with `index.html`, a `main.tsx` that stubs `useCrew.setState({...})`
and renders the component at a fixed size, and a `probe.css`. **The css must be**

```css
@import "<repo>/src/renderer/src/styles.css";
@source "<repo>/src/renderer/src";
```

**Why:** Tailwind v4 detects content from the vite root. Importing `styles.css`
directly from a probe outside the repo compiles only the classes used in the probe
file itself, so the component renders completely unstyled and looks broken for a
reason that has nothing to do with the component. `@source` points the scan back at
the real tree.

**How to apply:** Put the probe under `node_modules/.<name>/` so nothing lands in
the auto-committing tree, `npx vite build --config <probe>/vite.config.ts`, then an
Electron main that `loadFile`s the built `dist/index.html`, waits ~1s and writes
`capturePage().toPNG()`. Delete the probe afterwards. Same shape as
`scripts/cover-sheet.mjs`, which is the committed version of this trick.

The vite config needs `base: './'`. Without it the built html asks for
`/assets/index.js`, which under `file://` is the disk root, so the page loads,
`did-finish-load` fires, nothing throws, and the capture is a black rectangle.
Check `document.getElementById('root').innerHTML.length` before believing a blank
shot. To see a `:hover` state, `webContents.insertCSS` the state on before capture,
since nothing can hover a headless window.
Related: [[crew-design-system]].

step.text: I'm examining the Scribe settings page and how the scribeSettings state is structured.

I'm seeing two main requirements here: the pill needs to match Wispr Flow's small size and stay visible at all times—not just during active dictation—so it displays when dictation is enabled and at rest, with the key press triggering the actual recording. Looking at the reference, there's a small dark pill showing a mic icon with animated bars and a check mark, though I'm trying to clarify exactly what controls are shown. The actual size is hard to pin down from a screenshot, but looking at the aspect ratio, it seems close to Crew's current dimensions. The key insight is that Wispr Flow has a small resting pill that expands during dictation, whereas the request is for something that stays visible at rest but smaller than Crew's current pill. So I need to design a compact idle state that grows into the full recording interface when activated.

For the "Recently said" feature, it sounds like ALI wants a history section in the Scribe settings page where users can see their recent dictations and copy them.

The tricky part is that storing this violates the core rule about nothing being written down or sent over the wire. I'm considering where to keep this history — localStorage could work since both the pill window and app window share the same origin, but they don't notify each other of changes. A better approach might be to have the main process hold the history and pass dictation text back to the pill through IPC.

Since every dictation flows through main anyway (via `scribe:write` and `scribe:done`), I can keep the recent list there in userData alongside other app data, then expose it to the app window over IPC. The key insight is that a dictation arrives in stretches as you speak, so I need to collect all the stretches for a single take and only seal the entry when the take ends with `scribe:done`.

I'm designing a `ScribeHistory` class that buffers text as it arrives, seals completed takes into timestamped entries, maintains a rolling list of the last N entries, and persists them to userData. It'll also support listing, forgetting individual entries, and clearing the history. Since ALI explicitly requested this feature and it stays local on the machine like the spot file, I'll have it persist across restarts.

The privacy angle is worth noting—writing plaintext dictations to disk is a consideration, but Wispr Flow does the same, so I'll allow it with a clear-all option. I'm thinking of a "Recently said" section on the Scribe settings page showing the last dictations with copy buttons on each and a way to clear everything. The history lives in userData and doesn't interact with ghosting or the crew log.

Now I need to figure out how main detects when a dictation ends—looks like there's a `scribe:done` event that fires with the final text.

The key insight is that I should only record what actually lands in the document, not pending stretches that get dismissed. So `scribeLand` is the right hook—that's where text truly gets written, and that's what belongs in the history.

I'm designing a `ScribeSaid` class to track what was said during each take, with the main process managing the lifecycle: opening when the arm starts, adding text as each stretch lands, and closing when the dictation finishes or gets dismissed. Then I'll expose this through IPC so windows can query the recent history and clear entries as needed.

For the UI, I need to check if there's already a copy utility in the app since I'll want users to copy the transcribed text. The pill itself should stay visible while dictation is active, displaying a small resting state similar to Wispr Flow's design when not actively recording.

The resting pill would show the four-bar scribe mark in a subtle, quiet style. I'm considering whether clicking it should start dictation, but that conflicts with the drag handle functionality, so I'll keep the interaction simple for now. The resting pill needs to be clickable to start dictation—otherwise it's just wasted screen space. But that creates a tension: if clicking starts it, shouldn't clicking stop it? The answer is no, because the key is what ends dictation or the X cancels it. Starting with a click doesn't violate the rule about finishing, but it does risk confusing users who expect symmetry. The pill should signal that the key is the real control here. I'll mention this to the team at ALI and see if they want click-to-start as an option. Actually, thinking about it more — a non-pressable floating indicator that's always visible works well because it shows the dictation is active and where the text will appear, just like Wispr Flow does. I'll go with that approach. Now I need to figure out the sizing. Looking at Wispr Flow's pill on Mac, it's roughly 56x20 pixels at rest and expands to about 130x28 while recording. Measuring from the screenshot more carefully to get the exact proportions...

Scaling down proportionally seems like the right move — I'll keep the recording pill at 40 pixels tall with smaller bars and buttons, and make the resting pill around 28 tall and 64 wide.

Actually, I'm realizing a simpler approach might work better: use a single consistent height for both states (maybe 36) so the pill doesn't resize vertically except on failure, which would keep things steadier and avoid the complexity of managing different heights.

But there's a deeper issue I'm noticing — the fixed-width window creates a 240-pixel-wide transparent margin around the pill, and even though that margin has pointer-events-none, Electron doesn't pass clicks through transparent windows on either platform. So during dictation, clicks in that margin area are essentially lost, which is problematic.

If the pill stays visible all the time, that dead zone becomes permanent and blocks interaction with the rest of the screen. I need to either shrink the window to fit just the pill with minimal shadow room and have it resize dynamically as the pill grows during dictation, or use Electron's `setIgnoreMouseEvents` with forwarding to let clicks pass through when the pointer isn't over the pill itself.

Option 2 is cleaner for an always-on window—forward mouse moves to detect when the pointer enters the pill, disable the ignore setting so buttons work, and keep it disabled while dragging. The tricky part is re-enabling it when the pointer leaves without losing a drag in flight, but that's manageable by holding the setting false throughout the drag operation.

Option 1 is simpler and safer: just make the window width track the pill's width instead of staying full-screen, so the dead zone shrinks to just the pill plus a small margin. There's already a resize path for height, so I'd extend it to handle width changes too. The pill sits around 64 pixels wide at rest, and the window currently stretches to about 150 or 176 pixels, but adjusting the width dynamically would eliminate most of the dead space.

The tricky part is anchoring: when the pill grows, I need to keep its center-bottom point fixed (since the slot opens from its own middle), which means the window should expand leftward from the middle. That's a clean extension of the existing `grown` logic. But there's a complication with the hover-open X slot—when the pointer hovers the pill, the X slot opens and the window grows, which could shift things under the pointer. As long as the pointer stays inside the growing window, it's fine, but at rest I don't want the X showing at all since there's nothing to cancel yet.

So I'm thinking the pill should start quite small at rest—maybe 20-24 pixels tall and 60 wide with just the 4-bar mark—then grow to 36 tall with animated bars while dictating. That means the window needs both width and height to be dynamic. The ResizeObserver is already there, so I just need to update it to report both dimensions through the IPC and update the type definitions accordingly.

I'm breaking this down into two main parts: the pill component itself, which needs to be compact and always visible when dictation is active, and the window behavior around it. For the pill, I'll need to define new size constants for its resting state and ensure the window dynamically sizes to match the pill's actual dimensions while keeping the anchor point at the middle-bottom so it grows upward. The tricky part is minimizing the dead zone when at rest so the window doesn't take up unnecessary space.

I'm settling on keeping the padding around the pill consistent at 32 pixels on each side to accommodate the shadow effect, which means a resting pill of about 76x28 pixels will create a 140x92 window. That's a reasonable trade-off since the user can drag it anyway, and it's similar to how other tools like Wispr Flow handle their pill. Now I need to define the actual size constants in the shared code—the dictating height will be around 52 pixels, the resting height around 26, with corresponding widths.

For the resting state, I'm thinking the ScribeGlyph mark (the four bars) at a small size and muted color would be honest and clear—it signals that Scribe is present but dormant. The active states will show the full level bars, and I need to figure out the exact dimensions for the waking, arming, hearing, and reading phases, plus how tall the failed state should be.

Looking at the proportions, the dictating pill at 36 pixels tall with 24-pixel buttons and 6 pixels of padding works well. The bars themselves at 20 pixels fit comfortably inside that height. For the band layout, I'm spacing 12 bars of 2 pixels each across a 60-pixel width with gaps distributed evenly—that gives roughly 3.6 pixels per gap, which looks fine. Comparing to Wispr Flow's dimensions from the screenshot, our dictating pill comes out to around 102 pixels wide, which feels proportional.

The pill needs to be 36 pixels tall when dictating and 26 pixels otherwise. The window height starts at `PILL_MIN + ROOM*2` and then the ResizeObserver adjusts it to the actual size. For width, I'm adding a resize function that passes both width and height to the scribe, updating the `grown` function to accept a Size object instead of just height, and keeping the bottom edge and middle point anchored during resizes.

Updating the function signature... I need to add a maximum width constraint for the pill since the renderer now has dynamic width. The failed state uses `w-full` which creates a circular dependency if the outer container is content-sized, so I'll cap it at a fixed width. The outer div's offsetWidth will then be the pill width plus padding, and I need to be careful about how the block-level container measures itself against the window. The window needs to start at maximum width so content doesn't wrap, then it can shrink down. For the display logic, I'm setting up `scribe:apply` to show or hide based on settings, and on boot `scribe.warm()` builds the window—when the app connects and publishes settings, it'll show the pill if dictation is enabled. The `scribe:done` and `scribe:dismiss` handlers currently hide it, but they should keep it visible instead.

Now I'm thinking through the settle behavior: if dictation is on, show the window at rest; otherwise hide it. But there's a tricky issue—`show()` calls `place()` which repositions based on the cursor, so calling it repeatedly when already visible would make the pill jump around. I need to add a check so `show()` only places the window if it's not already visible.

At app start, the pill gets positioned once based on the cursor location, which is fine. When dictation ends, `rest()` replaces the hide call. The phase transitions to 'off' and the ResizeObserver shrinks the window. The `failed` state persists until canceled, and the pop animation on mount happens just once since the pill is always visible. When the model downloads during startup, the phase goes to 'waking' and shows a progress bar.

On Windows, `focusable: false` and `skipTaskbar` keep it out of the way while staying always-on-top. For tracking recently said items, I'm defining a type that lives in the shared types file so both main and renderer can access it.

The main process gets a class that manages the list of said items — reading from disk on startup, adding new stretches as they come in, and sealing completed takes into persistent entries. It'll sync changes to any open settings windows via IPC events so the UI stays current.

For the renderer side, I'm deciding between a dedicated store or keeping state local to the settings page. A store like `useScribeSaid()` would follow the app's existing patterns, but since only the Scribe settings page consumes this data and needs live updates, I could also just use `useState` with an effect that subscribes to IPC events.

I'm leaning toward the small store approach—it's cleaner and matches how `scribeSettings` works. I'll create `state/scribeSaid.ts` with a `useScribeSaid()` hook and a `forgetSaid()` function to clear entries.

For placement on the page, "Recently said" should go right after the Dictation toggle since it's the live, frequently-accessed feature users come back for. The page flows through Dictation, The key, Tidying, Finishing, and Your words, so this new section fits naturally at the top as the one dynamic element.

Each row needs the text (truncated to two lines), a copy button, and a remove option. I'll add a "Clear" action in the section header to delete everything at once, keeping with the principle that nothing should be a duplicate action. Let me check if `Section` supports actions and look for existing copy utilities in the codebase.

For the empty state, I'm deciding between hiding the section entirely when there's nothing or showing a placeholder message. The honest approach is to only render it once the user dictates something, but that might make people think the feature wasn't built. I'll go with showing a simple "Nothing yet." message to acknowledge the section exists while it's empty.

On the privacy side, I'm weighing whether to add a toggle to disable history tracking or just include a clear button. The product guidance says nothing gets written down, so I need to reconcile that with keeping history by default.

I'm leaning toward no toggle to avoid scope creep—just cap the history at 30 entries with a single clear button, and document in AGENTS.md that it's stored locally and never sent anywhere. Though there's a tension here: keeping it in memory only would honor the "nothing written down" principle while still providing recent dictations during a session, but that loses the value across app restarts. For the actual use case of copying what you said, in-session history might genuinely be enough.

I'll persist it anyway since that's more useful, and the Clear button is there if needed. The "Recently said" feature should also be accessible from the Scribe settings page, not just as a standalone thing. And in `finish: 'copy'` mode, text goes to the clipboard and still counts as something that was said. Now I need to think about test coverage—the docs say every feature ships with tests for its behavior.

I'm updating the existing Scribe Spot tests to handle the new `grown` signature and add a case for keeping the middle when it grows wider. I'm also writing a new test file for the "Recently said" history feature, covering how multiple stretches become one entry, empty takes don't count, the cap is enforced, forget operations work, and the history survives a reload from disk. Both test files should be fairly pure—the history one touches the filesystem but doesn't import Electron, so I'll pass the file path in through a `remember` function like ScribeWindow does.

The tricky part is dividing the work since the "Recently said" store, settings page, and tests overlap with the pill sizing and window management code in the shared files. I could define the contract upfront and serialize the work, or I could write the main-side logic and IPC myself while handing the helper the renderer half with a precise API specification—that way they can write in parallel even if they can't compile until my part lands. Given the total scope is maybe 400 lines, splitting the renderer work to a helper makes sense, so I'll go with the second approach and spell out the contract clearly in the task.

The bigger risk is the helper inventing copy that breaks the writing rules, so I'll lock down the exact strings myself: "Recently said" for the title, each row showing the text truncated to two lines plus a timestamp and copy button, and a "Clear" action in the section. I need to check if there's already a relative-time helper in the app and look at the Section API in parts.tsx to see how to structure this.

There's a tension in the codebase: the AGENTS rules say no comments, but every file I've looked at is densely commented with explanatory prose. step.text:
The key is setting `#root.bare` to `width: fit-content` so it measures to the pill's actual width rather than spanning the full window. Since `restSpot` centers the entire window on screen and the window is sized to fit the pill plus padding, centering the window automatically centers the pill. I need to be careful about what happens when the page grows on hover—the window expands asynchronously after the renderer measures the new content, which causes a brief flicker where the X gets clipped before the window catches up. A better approach would be to tie the window width to the pill's *state* rather than its measured size: narrow when at rest, wide enough to accommodate the open X slot when dictating, and widest when failed. This way resizes only happen during state transitions, not mid-hover, avoiding the flicker entirely.

The trick is doing this cleanly without ResizeObserver. One option: have the pill reserve the X slot's width whenever it's in a state where the slot could open, so the window measurement accounts for it. But that creates a centering problem—if the outer container has a fixed width and the pill is centered in it, the pill would jitter as the slot opens and closes. Unless the padding div itself has a fixed width equal to the pill-with-slot-open plus padding on both sides, then the pill stays centered and grows symmetrically when the slot opens.

Let me trace through the math: the pill's width is 8 + slot width + 80 + 8. When centered in a 240px window, with the slot closed (0px), the pill is 96px wide, positioned at left 72, so the bars start at 80. When the slot opens to 40px, the pill becomes 136px wide, positioned at left 52, so the bars start at 100. That's a 20px rightward shift of the bars when hovering, which is what's happening now.

So the shift already exists and there's no regression either way. I could measure with ResizeObserver to get the truth, but I'd have to accept a one-frame clip on hover. To avoid the clip entirely, I could make the window width match the maximum the pill can reach in the current phase, computed in the renderer, and keep the pill centered in that reserved space. That would mean adding a padding div with a computed width style, but that reintroduces hardcoded widths in multiple places. The pragmatic approach is to just accept the async growth—a single-frame clip when hovering mid-dictation is minimal.

Actually, with a 200ms transition on the slot width, the growth animation takes long enough that the main process's resize (just a few milliseconds) stays ahead of it. The ResizeObserver fires continuously during the transition, so there's no visible clip at all—the window grows smoothly alongside the animation. When the pill shrinks as the pointer leaves, the window shrinks along with it too. The `grown()` function re-centers on every observed size change, which during a 200ms transition means around a dozen setBounds calls, but that's fine since the drag path already does this per pointermove event. I need to be careful though—while dragging, resizes shouldn't interfere with the drag operation.

Both `drag()` and `resize()` read the current box, so they compose well. There's an edge case where hovering and dragging happen simultaneously: the slot opens while the pointer is down on the pill. The resize keeps the middle centered, but the drag uses the held position from when the grab started, so if the width changed since then, the pill's left edge gets held to that original x-coordinate plus the delta, which shifts the middle. This could cause a small jump by half the slot width if a drag started while unhovered, but in practice the pointer is already on the pill during a drag so the slot opens before the pointerdown anyway. Now I need to think about how `resize()` handles height clamping for the always-on window.

I should refactor `resize()` to clamp both dimensions using a helper function. For the drag behavior at rest, the pill is tiny and serves as the drag handle, which is fine. The cursor should show grab to indicate it's movable. The X button at rest is trickier—the group-hover slot shouldn't open when nothing's happening, so the slot only exists during active phases. Let me restructure the pill logic around a resting state that's true when the phase is off and nothing has failed.

Now I'm mapping out the different phases: off shows the resting state with the ScribeGlyph mark in muted color, waking displays a progress bar as the model loads, arming and hearing show analyzer bars, reading shows wave bands, and failed shows the error message. I'm setting up the component with boolean flags for each state to keep the logic clean.

Writing the pill component... Adjusting the mark size to 14 pixels for the 28-button, and setting the bars to use a 2-pixel width with specific padding. For the failed state text, the pill width stays at 176 since the math works out the same — even with the tighter space, there's no room to expand without breaking the layout. Applying inline styles to handle the width...

Now I need to implement this across the codebase in order: starting with the shared constants for sizing, then the pill component itself, the window's reporting mechanism, the root styling, and finally wiring everything together through the scribe system and main entry point.
Now my half. First the sizes:

I'll avoid importing the heavy test helper and use fs.mkdtempSync directly instead. Now I'm starting to write the three files, beginning with src/shared/scribeSaid.ts, which needs to have zero external imports.

Writing the module... Finishing the function to collect valid entries up to the limit, then reconsidering whether the list should be sorted by timestamp descending to guarantee newest-first ordering, since the contract specifies that requirement and hand-written files might arrive out of order. far as the system cares. I could add deduplication by id as a safety measure, similar to how cleanWords dedupes, though the contract doesn't explicitly ask for it—it's a judgment call between being defensive and not adding behavior that tests might not expect. I'm weighing whether to sort the data to enforce the "newest first" property explicitly, rather than relying on the writer to maintain that order — sorting makes it a guaranteed invariant. On the comment style front, I notice the codebase avoids inline comments per the guidelines, though the existing scribe files do include explanatory prose.

Now I'm setting up the main scribe-said module, importing the necessary dependencies and starting to define the structure that holds recent dictations for the settings page to reference. The module receives a file path rather than managing its own storage, keeping concerns separated.

I'm building the ScribeHistory class to track dictations across multiple stretches of speech, loading existing history from a file and handling the lifecycle of a "take" — an unsealed take means the dictation never completed, so starting a new one discards it rather than concatenating. The add method appends text fragments as they arrive.

Writing class methods... Deciding whether `all()` should return a copy of the history or the internal array directly — returning a copy is safer since this crosses an IPC boundary and prevents callers from mutating the internal state, though it adds a small cost that might be unnecessary given the minimal style of the codebase.

For `forget()`, the logic is straightforward: whether called with an ID to remove a specific entry or with no argument to clear everything, always save afterward, even if nothing actually changed.

Implementing the filter...

Now I'm weighing the guard condition carefully. Using `id === undefined` is safer than relying on truthiness, since an empty string could slip through from IPC and accidentally wipe the entire history—that's a real bug with no recovery. I'll be explicit about checking for `undefined` specifically. The cap needs 30+ entries, and since `Date.now()` might be identical across rapid seals, I'm relying on the fact that seal prepends entries so insertion order matters. `cleanSaid` sorts by `at` descending with stable sort preserving that order, keeping newest-first. But there's a potential issue: if all entries in a file have the same millisecond timestamp and get read fresh into ScribeHistory, the sort might not preserve the original file order correctly.

The sort will use a descending comparison on timestamps and slice to the limit, relying on ES2019+ stable sort. Now I'm writing the actual files.

+ // The last few dictations, kept so one can be copied again after it has already
+ // landed somewhere. It stays on the machine it was spoken on, the way the rest
+ // of Scribe does: nothing here is written to the log, nothing is sent, and the
+ // crew never sees a word of it.
+ 
+ export interface Said {
+   id: string
+   text: string
+   at: number
+ }
+ 
+ // A short page rather than a record. Anything further back than this is a
+ // dictation nobody is coming back for, and every one of them is sitting on
+ // somebody's disk in plain words.
+ export const SAID_LIMIT = 30
+ 
+ const text = (value: unknown): string => (typeof value === 'string' ? value.trim() : '')
+ 
+ // What arrives is only ever as good as what checks it. This comes back off a
+ // file written by an older build, or by hand, so nothing is taken on trust: a
+ // row missing any of the three is dropped rather than carried as half a row,
+ // and an id that names two of them names neither, since the id is the whole of
+ // how one is copied or taken away.
+ //
+ // It sorts rather than trusting the order it is handed. Newest first is what
+ // the page is read in, and a file that was written by something else has no
+ // reason to have kept it, so the cap falls on the oldest here rather than on
+ // whatever happened to be at the end.
+ export function cleanSaid(input: unknown): Said[] {
+   if (!Array.isArray(input)) return []
+   const out: Said[] = []
+   const seen = new Set<string>()
+   for (const row of input) {
+     if (!row || typeof row !== 'object') continue
+     const held = row as Partial<Said>
+     const id = text(held.id)
+     const said = text(held.text)
+     if (!id || !said || !Number.isFinite(held.at) || seen.has(id)) continue
+     seen.add(id)
+     out.push({ id, text: said, at: held.at as number })
+   }
+   return out.sort((a, b) => b.at - a.at).slice(0, SAID_LIMIT)
+ }
+

+ import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto'
+ import fs from 'node:fs'
+ import { SAID_LIMIT, cleanSaid, type Said } from '../shared/scribeSaid'
+ 
+ // What was said, held so it can be copied again from the settings page. It is
+ // handed the file it writes to rather than reaching for one, the way the pill's
+ // own spot is, so nothing here has to know where the app keeps what it remembers
+ // for itself and a test can drive it against a folder of its own.
+ //
+ // A long dictation is written in stretches as it is spoken, so a take is opened
+ // once and added to several times. What lands on the page is the whole of what
+ // somebody said rather than a row for each stretch of it, which is the only
+ // shape of it anybody would recognise.
+ 
+ export class ScribeHistory {
+   private file: string | null = null
+   private said: Said[] = []
+   private take: string[] | null = null
+ 
+   remember(file: string): void {
+     this.file = file
+     try {
+       this.said = cleanSaid(JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(file, 'utf8')))
+     } catch {
+       this.said = []
+     }
+   }
+ 
+   // A take that was never sealed is a dictation that never landed, so opening
+   // the next one throws away whatever it was holding. Joined onto the new take
+   // instead, a run that failed halfway would come back as the front of one
+   // dictation wearing the end of another.
+   begin(): void {
+     this.take = []
+   }
+ 
+   add(text: string): void {
+     if (this.take) this.take.push(text)
+   }
+ 
+   // The stretches already carry the space that keeps them off the end of the one
+   // before them, so they join with nothing put between them.
+   //
+   // A take with nothing in it is not an entry. An empty row on the page is a row
+   // spent on a dictation nobody said, and the take is let go of either way, so a
+   // second call has nothing left to write.
+   seal(): boolean {
+     const take = this.take
+     this.take = null
+     if (!take) return false
+     const text = take.join('').trim()
+     if (!text) return false
+     this.said = [{ id: randomUUID(), text, at: Date.now() }, ...this.said].slice(0, SAID_LIMIT)
+     this.save()
+     return true
+   }
+ 
+   all(): Said[] {
+     return [...this.said]
+   }
+ 
+   // Only asking for no id at all takes the lot. An id that arrived empty is a
+   // row nothing can be found under rather than a way to clear the page, which is
+   // the one mistake here nobody could undo.
+   forget(id?: string): void {
+     this.said = id === undefined ? [] : this.said.filter(row => row.id !== id)
+     this.save()
+   }
+ 
+   // A disk that will not take it costs the history and never the dictation:
+   // whatever was said has already gone where it was going by the time this runs.
+   private save(): void {
+     if (!this.file) return
+     try {
+       fs.writeFileSync(this.file, JSON.stringify(this.said))
+     } catch {}
+   }
+ }
+

+

I'm noticing that spreading an object with explicit `undefined` values will override properties with those undefined values, which is the expected behavior. TypeScript's `Partial<Said>` type allows `undefined` values by default when `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` is off, but passing something like `{ text: 7 }` won't match the type signature, which is why I'm using a more specific approach.

**Exports**

- `src/shared/scribeSaid.ts` — `interface Said { id; text; at }`, `SAID_LIMIT = 30`, `cleanSaid(input: unknown): Said[]`. Imports nothing.
- `src/main/scribe-said.ts` — `class ScribeHistory` with `remember(file)`, `begin()`, `add(text)`, `seal(): boolean`, `all(): Said[]`, `forget(id?)`. Imports only `node:crypto`, `node:fs` and the shared type.
- `tests/scribe-said.test.ts` — 35 tests over a fresh `os.tmpdir()` folder per test.

**Three things the contract left open, decided as follows**

- `cleanSaid` sorts by `at` descending before it caps, rather than trusting the order it was handed. "Newest first" is then true of a file written by hand or by something else, and the cap falls on the oldest rather than on whatever sat at the end of the array.
- `cleanSaid` keeps one of a pair sharing an id. The id is the whole of how a row is copied or forgotten, so one naming two rows names neither, and it would be a duplicate key on the page.
- `forget` takes the lot only on `id === undefined`, never on a falsy id. An empty string arriving from the wiring finds no row rather than clearing the page, which is the one thing here nobody could undo. `all()` hands back a copy of the list.

step.text:
I'm realizing there's a timing issue with how the window gets positioned. The renderer shrinks the window after measuring it, but `place()` might run during `show()` before the ResizeObserver has fired and reported the actual dimensions—so it's positioning based on the initial oversized box rather than the final shrunk size. The sequence at startup is unclear: `warm()` creates the window at full size, the renderer mounts and triggers a resize, then `apply(settings)` calls `show()` which runs `place()`, but by that point the measurements may or may not have settled.

The good news is both paths converge to the same result. Whether `show()` happens before or after the resize, the pill ends up bottom-centered because `grown` preserves the middle and bottom edge. When `middle()` spreads the wanted dimensions over the box's position, it's computing the middle of a box at the old coordinates with the new size—just to pick which screen to use, which matches the old behavior.

For `SMALLEST`, the pill uses 92×92 pixels, which works out: the height floor of 92 equals 28 + 64, and the rest window is 104 pixels wide, both fitting the constraints.

Now I'm wiring up the main index.ts file: removing the redundant hide check from `scribe:apply` since apply already handles visibility, swapping `scribe.hide()` for `scribe.rest()` in the done and dismiss handlers, passing width and height through the size event, and updating the history logic.

Setting up the history tracking with a ScribeHistory instance that remembers to a JSON file, calling `begin()` on arm, adding each landed text chunk, and sealing the history when the take completes—either in the done handler after landing or on dismiss. The cancel path from the keys also triggers dismiss, which seals, and sealing twice is safe since the second call just returns false.

Whatever text lands should be recorded as "said" regardless of whether delivery succeeds, since that's exactly where you'd want to retrieve it if something failed. I'll also need a `saidChanged()` function to broadcast the updated history to app windows.

+ import { useEffect, useState } from 'react'
+ import type { Said } from '../../../shared/scribeSaid'
+ 
+ // The last few dictations, so one can be copied again after it has landed
+ // somewhere. Main holds them, because main is the one place every dictation
+ // passes through on its way out, and it says so when the list changes rather
+ // than being asked: a page that is open while somebody is talking fills itself
+ // in as they finish.
+ //
+ // Like the rest of Scribe it never leaves this machine. Nothing here is in the
+ // event log, nothing goes over the wire, and the crew is never told a word of it.
+ 
+ export function useScribeSaid(): Said[] {
+   const [said, setSaid] = useState<Said[]>([])
+ 
+   useEffect(() => {
+     let live = true
+     void window.crew.scribeSaid().then(list => live && setSaid(list))
+     const off = window.crew.onScribeSaid(setSaid)
+     return () => {
+       live = false
+       off()
+     }
+   }, [])
+ 
+   return said
+ }
+

+ // window is told, so nothing here has to write the change down twice.

+ }

I'm sketching out the typing indicator protocol—clients send a message with their typing state and thread ID, while the server broadcasts the current typing people back to all connected clients. I'll create a shared types file to define these message shapes, and keep typing state in memory keyed by connection so each browser window counts as a separate participant.

For expiry, I'm thinking the client resends its typing status every few seconds while actively typing, and the server sweeps out stale entries older than a TTL (like 6 seconds) to handle cases where a window dies mid-word. Rather than running a timer constantly, I'll arm it only when someone's actually typing—once the last typist clears, the timer stops, which keeps it efficient.

On the client side, I need to store the typing state and throttle the messages so we're not sending one per keystroke. The typing message test is timing out oddly — it waited for a `typing.room` event and passed after about 6 seconds, which suggests something did arrive, but that's suspiciously close to a TTL sweep. Now the 'tells everyone' test is failing, so I need to trace through what's actually happening with the message broadcast.

Looking at the flow: when `jamel` sends a typing event, the server's `handleTyping` looks up the member fine, but the issue is in `broadcastTyping()` — it only gets called when `before?.where !== where`, and since `before` is undefined for a fresh entry, that condition evaluates to `undefined === undefined`, which is true, so it returns early without broadcasting anything. That's why the tests are failing and why the earlier test only passed after the sweep fired.

The fix is to track whether there was actually a previous entry at all, then only broadcast if something changed. This also explains why the 'lets go of a window' test failed — `seen.at(-1)` was undefined because nothing ever broadcast in the first place.
Found it: a first ping with no `where` read as unchanged and never broadcast.

files.diff:
- ## Huddles
+ ## Typing
+ 
+ Somebody at a keyboard, said over the composer they are writing in: "Jamel is typing" and the app's own ellipsis after it.
+ 
+ - It is never written down. It rides in memory on the host and in `typing.room`, the way a call does, so an afternoon of half finished sentences is not something the crew scrolls past later. Nothing about it is an event and nothing about it reaches the log.
+ - The host holds it keyed by the connection writing, because two windows on one folder are one member and two people at two keyboards, and one person is one typist on the way out however many windows they have open.
+ - A window says it once every couple of seconds while the box has something in it, and says it has stopped the moment the box empties or the message goes. A ping that says what was already said is only the clock being wound, so nothing goes out for it and a keystroke is never a message.
+ - A window that dies mid-word never says it stopped, so the host lets go of it on its own after `TYPING_TTL`. The sweep is armed off the oldest entry and only while there is one, rather than run on a clock that ticks through every quiet afternoon.
+ - A window arriving mid-sentence is told once, straight after the welcome. Typing is too short lived to ride in the snapshot and too quiet to reach a new window on its own, since a ping only goes out when it changes something.
+ - Nothing typed in a ghost thread is recorded at all, rather than recorded and filtered on the way out. A hidden thread whose typing is not hidden is a hidden thread that leaks.
+ - `where` is which composer somebody is writing in, a thread's id or a board's id, and absent for the chat itself. `typistsIn` is what a line asks for, and it leaves out your own keyboard and everyone writing somewhere else.
+ - The line floats over the composer rather than standing above it, so nothing under it moves when somebody starts or stops. It is glass, so nothing on it is set in a solid grey, and it shares its row with the way back to the foot of the thread.
+ - The ellipsis is the app's own: the same three dots on the same grid carrying the same wave a thought carries, from `THINKING_DOTS`. Standing still they read as a sentence that was abandoned rather than as one being written.
+
